agent.howItWorksBody: The {{name}} agent is a small daemon that runs on the host and forwards local events to UTMStack over an authenticated TLS connection. It auto-updates and reports its health.
agent.installHint: Run this command on every {{name}} host you want to monitor. The token already encodes your current workspace.
agent.after1: The host appears under Data Sources within ~60 seconds of agent start.
agent.after2: Telemetry begins flowing into Log Explorer, scoped to your workspace.
agent.after3: The agent self-reports CPU / memory / disk health back to UTMStack.
agent.noRemoteControl: Disable remote command execution on this host
agent.prereqBody: The UTMStack agent communicates with the server over the following ports. Make sure they are open between the host and UTMStack before installing:
agent.sensitiveWarning: The command below contains a sensitive enrollment token — do not share it.

uninstall.title: Uninstall the agent
uninstall.body: Run this on the host to stop and remove the UTMStack agent and its services. It uses the platform selected above.

agent.macCompat: Requires macOS 11 (Big Sur) or later on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3 or newer). Intel-based Macs are not supported.

collector.howItWorksBody: {{name}} doesn't run a UTMStack agent. Instead, you install the UTMStack collector somewhere on the network that both your {{name}} device and UTMStack can reach. {{name}} sends syslog to the collector, the collector parses, normalizes, and forwards events into UTMStack.
collector.step1Hint: Run on a Linux host with network access from the {{name}} device.
collector.step2Hint: On the {{name}} device, point syslog forwarding to the collector's address on {{port}}.
collector.step3Body: Within a few minutes you should see {{name}} events under source: {{source}} in Log Explorer, and a new entry in Data Sources.

endpoint.title: Connection details
endpoint.hint: Configure {{name}} to forward its logs to the Collector using the host and port below.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: The AS/400 Collector is a Linux service that connects directly to your AS/400 (IBM i) systems and pulls security journal entries, then streams them securely to UTMStack for correlation and alerting.
intro.note: Nothing is installed on the AS/400 itself — the Collector runs on a Linux host that has network access to your AS/400 systems.

install.title: Install the AS/400 Collector
install.body: Run this command on a Linux host that can reach both UTMStack and your AS/400 systems over the network.
install.reuse: Already have the AS/400 Collector installed? Skip this step — just add your servers to the configuration file in the next step.

configure.title: Add your AS/400 servers
configure.body: Edit as400-config.yaml in the collector's installation directory and add each AS/400 system you want to monitor:
configure.note: You can list multiple servers. The collector watches this file and reloads automatically on save — no restart needed.

journal.title: Enable audit journaling on AS/400
journal.body: On each AS/400 system, make sure the <hl>QAUDJRN</hl> security audit journal is active. Refer to IBM's documentation for the exact steps — the procedure varies between IBM i versions.

uninstall.title: Optional — Uninstall the Collector
uninstall.body: Run this command on the host where the AS/400 Collector is installed to stop the service and remove all files.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack connects to Bitdefender GravityZone using your API key to configure the Event Push Service. GravityZone then sends security events directly to UTMStack for correlation and alerting.
intro.note: No agent is installed on GravityZone — UTMStack registers itself as the push destination using read-only API credentials.

whitelist.title: Whitelist Bitdefender IPs
whitelist.body: The following Bitdefender GravityZone IP addresses must be allowed through your firewall on port 8000 so that the Event Push Service can reach UTMStack:
whitelist.note: Add these IPs to your firewall or security group before completing the setup.

myAccount.title: Open My Account
myAccount.body: In the Bitdefender GravityZone console, click on My Account.

accessUrl.title: Note the Access URL
accessUrl.body: Scroll down to the Control Center API section and save the Access URL — you will enter it in the credentials form below. Then open the API key section and click Add at the top of the table.

createKey.title: Create an API key
createKey.body: Write a description for the API key, select the Event Push Service API option, and click Save. Copy the generated key.

myCompany.title: Open My Company
myCompany.body: In the GravityZone console, click on My Company.

licensing.title: Note the Company IDs
licensing.body: Open the Licensing section and save the Company IDs you want to monitor — enter them comma-separated in the credentials form below.

credentials.title: Enter credentials
credentials.body: Fill in the Access URL, API key, your UTMStack public IP (where GravityZone will push events), and the Company IDs to monitor. UTMStack verifies the credentials before saving.

step1.title: Enable the ESET listener on the Collector
step1.body: On the host where the Collector is installed, run this command to open the ESET syslog listener:
step1.note: To use TCP instead of UDP, replace udp with tcp in the command above.

moreMenu.title: Open the More menu
moreMenu.body: In the ESET Protect console sidebar, click the <hl>More</hl> menu.

serverConfig.title: Open Server settings
serverConfig.body: Under More, open the <hl>Server settings</hl> (Server configuration) section.

advanced.title: Expand Advanced settings
advanced.body: Click <hl>Advanced settings</hl> to expand the full list of configuration options.

syslog.title: Configure the Syslog server
syslog.body: Scroll to <hl>Syslog server</hl>, enable <hl>Export logs to Syslog</hl>, and set the destination to the Collector host on port {{port}} (UDP). ESET sends LEEF/syslog, which the Collector ingests as the antivirus-esmc-eset data type.

step1.title: Enable the Kaspersky listener on the Collector
step1.body: On the host where the Collector is installed, run this command to open the Kaspersky syslog listener:
step1.note: To use TCP instead of UDP, replace udp with tcp in the command above.

consoleSettings.title: Open Console settings → Integration
consoleSettings.body: In the Kaspersky Security Center sidebar, open <hl>Console settings</hl> and click the <hl>Integration</hl> submenu.

siem.title: Open the SIEM integration settings
siem.body: Under Integration, select <hl>SIEM</hl> and click the <hl>Settings</hl> link to open the export configuration.

configure.title: Configure the SIEM export
configure.body: Enable export and set Kaspersky to send events in <hl>Splunk (CEF)</hl> format to the Collector host on port {{port}} (UDP). The Collector ingests them as the antivirus-kaspersky data type.

intro.title: Sophos Central — API Plugin
intro.body: Sophos Central provides secure APIs to retrieve event and alert data. UTMStack connects to those APIs to centralize monitoring and enhance your security visibility — no agent or collector required.
intro.note: UTMStack polls the Sophos Central API on a schedule. Ensure the API credentials you create below have read access to events and alerts.

sophos.apiSection: Generate API Credentials in Sophos Central

apiCredentials.title: Open API Credentials Management
apiCredentials.body: In <hl>Sophos Central Admin</hl>, navigate to <hl>Global Settings → API Credentials Management</hl>.

addCredential.title: Create a new credential
addCredential.body: Click <hl>Add Credential</hl>. Provide a <hl>Name</hl> and <hl>Description</hl>, select the appropriate <hl>Role</hl>, then click <hl>Add</hl>.

copyIds.title: Copy Client ID and Client Secret
copyIds.body: Copy the <hl>Client ID</hl> and <hl>Client Secret</hl> and store them securely.
copyIds.secretNote: The Client Secret is shown only once. Save it somewhere safe before closing this dialog.

credentials.title: Add Sophos Central credentials
credentials.body: Enter the credentials you just created. You can add more than one Sophos account by clicking Add config group.

login.title: 1 · Log in to the management console
login.body: Log in to the Webroot management console. It opens on the Sites tab.

apiAccess.title: 3 · Open API Access
apiAccess.body: From the Subscriptions tab, click on the API Access tab.

createCredential.title: 4 · Create a client credential
createCredential.body: Click New and fill in the Name and Description. Read the SecureAnywhere Business Solution and Unity API agreement, then click Create.

noteClientSecret.title: 5 · Copy the client ID and secret
noteClientSecret.body: Save the Client ID from the list and the Client Secret that's shown only once. Click "I have made note of the client secret" to confirm.

fillForm.title: 6 · Fill the form
fillForm.body: Provide the client ID and client secret to UTMStack. You can add more than one Webroot config group if needed.

activate.title: 7 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so Webroot events start flowing.

step1.title: Enable the SentinelOne listener on the Collector
step1.body: On the host where the Collector is installed, run this command to open the SentinelOne syslog listener. SentinelOne streams CEF over TCP:
step1.note: For an encrypted channel use tls instead of tcp (load certificates on the Collector first).

settings.title: Open the SentinelOne Settings
settings.body: In the SentinelOne management console sidebar, click the <hl>Settings</hl> menu.

syslog.title: Configure the Syslog integration
syslog.body: Go to <hl>Integrations → Syslog</hl> and enable it. Set the host to <hl>{{host}}</hl> and port to <hl>{{port}}</hl>, keep the format as <hl>CEF</hl>, click <hl>Test</hl> to verify the connection, then <hl>Save</hl>.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack connects to Microsoft 365 using a registered Azure AD app and polls the Office 365 Management Activity API for audit and security events. No agent is installed in your tenant.
intro.note: UTMStack requires read-only API access — no write permissions are requested.

azurePortal.title: Open Microsoft Entra ID
azurePortal.body: Open the <hl>Azure Portal</hl> (portal.azure.com) and click on <hl>Microsoft Entra ID</hl>.

appRegistrations.title: Go to App registrations
appRegistrations.body: In the left menu, click <hl>App registrations</hl>.

registerApp.title: Register a new app
registerApp.body: Click <hl>New registration</hl>. Name it <hl>UTMStack O365 Agent</hl>, select <hl>Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single-tenant)</hl>, and click <hl>Register</hl>.

clientSecret.title: Create a client secret
clientSecret.body: Go to <hl>Certificates & Secrets → New client secret</hl>. Add a description, set expiry to <hl>730 days (24 months)</hl>, and click <hl>Add</hl>.
clientSecret.copyNote: Copy the secret Value immediately — it is only shown once and cannot be retrieved later.

apiPermissions.title: Add Office 365 Management API permissions
apiPermissions.body: Go to <hl>API Permissions → Add a permission</hl> and search for <hl>Office 365 Management APIs</hl>.

activityFeed.title: Grant ActivityFeed permissions
activityFeed.body: Select <hl>Application Permissions</hl> and add <hl>ActivityFeed.Read</hl> and <hl>ActivityFeed.ReadDlp</hl>. Click <hl>Grant admin consent</hl> and confirm.

graphPermissions.title: Add Microsoft Graph permissions
graphPermissions.body: Back in <hl>Add a permission</hl>, click <hl>Microsoft Graph</hl>.

delegatedPermissions.title: Add delegated SecurityAlert permissions
delegatedPermissions.body: Select <hl>Delegated Permissions</hl> and add <hl>SecurityAlert.Read.All</hl> and <hl>SecurityAlert.ReadWrite.All</hl>. Click <hl>Grant admin consent</hl> and confirm.

appPermissions.title: Add application SecurityAlert permissions
appPermissions.body: Select <hl>Application Permissions</hl> and add <hl>SecurityAlert.Read.All</hl> and <hl>SecurityAlert.ReadWrite.All</hl>. Click <hl>Grant admin consent</hl> and confirm.

noteIds.title: Copy the app IDs
noteIds.body: Go to the app <hl>Overview</hl> and copy the <hl>Application (client) ID</hl> and <hl>Directory (tenant) ID</hl>. You also need the secret value copied in step 4.

credentials.title: Connect your Microsoft 365 tenant
credentials.body: Enter the details from the steps above. UTMStack verifies the credentials before saving. You can add multiple config groups.

step1.title: Enable the GitHub webhook listener on the Collector
step1.body: On the host where the Collector is installed, run this command to open the HTTPS webhook listener for GitHub:
step1.tokenNote: The terminal will print a secret token — copy it immediately. It will not be shown again.

certWarning.title: GitHub requires a CA-signed TLS certificate
certWarning.body: GitHub only delivers webhooks to HTTPS endpoints with a certificate issued by a public CA (self-signed certificates are rejected). Make sure the Collector host has a valid domain certificate before registering the webhook.

step2.title: Register the webhook in GitHub
step2.body: In your repository or organization, go to Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook and fill in the form:
step2.secretHint: Paste the <hl>token</hl> shown when the integration was enabled above.
step2.eventsHint: Send me everything — or select specific event types.

openSetup.title: 1 · Open Setup
openSetup.body: Go to Setup and select "Setup for the current app" at the top right of the screen.

appManager.title: 2 · Open App Manager
appManager.body: Type "App Manager" in the quick search box and select App Manager.

newConnectedApp.title: 3 · Create a new Connected App
newConnectedApp.body: On the Lightning Experience App Manager screen, click "New Connected App" and fill in the fields.

oauthSettings.title: 4 · Enable OAuth Settings
oauthSettings.body: In the "API (Enable OAuth Settings)" section, check "Enable OAuth Settings" and use https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/success as the Callback URL.

oauthScopes.title: 5 · Add OAuth scopes
oauthScopes.body: Select "Access Connect REST API resources (chatter_api)" under Selected OAuth Scopes.

save.title: 6 · Save
save.body: Save your changes and select Continue on the next screen.

manageConsumer.title: 7 · Open Manage Consumer Details
manageConsumer.body: Inside your Connected App, go to "API (Enable OAuth Settings)" and click "Manage Consumer Details" next to Consumer Key and Secret.

copyCredentials.title: 8 · Copy the consumer key and secret
copyCredentials.body: Verify your identity. The Consumer Key and Consumer Secret appear under "Consumer Details". Copy both with the Copy button.

fillForm.title: 9 · Fill the form
fillForm.body: Provide the Consumer Key, Consumer Secret, Salesforce username and password to UTMStack.

activate.title: 10 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so Salesforce events start flowing.

enableModule.title: 1 · Enable the IIS Filebeat module
enableModule.body:
On the UTMStack agent host, run:
cd "C:\Program Files\UTMStack\UTMStack Agent\beats\filebeat\" && filebeat modules enable iis

configureModule.title: 2 · Configure the IIS module
configureModule.body: Edit C:\Program Files\UTMStack\UTMStack Agent\beats\filebeat\modules.d\iis.yml as shown below to point at the IIS log directories you want to ship.

activate.title: 3 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so IIS events start flowing.

installRsyslog.title: 1 · Install rsyslog
installRsyslog.body: Ensure rsyslog is installed on the host. Use your distribution's package manager (apt, dnf, yum).

configureRsyslog.title: 2 · Configure rsyslog to forward to UTMStack
configureRsyslog.body: Edit /etc/rsyslog.conf (or a file under /etc/rsyslog.d/) and add a forwarding rule that targets the UTMStack agent over UDP or TCP on port 514.

restartRsyslog.title: 3 · Restart rsyslog
restartRsyslog.body: Restart the rsyslog service: sudo systemctl restart rsyslog

enableCollector.title: 4 · Enable the Linux logs collector
enableCollector.body: Enable the log collector and the Linux Logs integration in the configuration file where your UTMStack agent is installed.

overview.title: 1 · Use the HTTP/JSON ingestion endpoint
overview.body: UTMStack accepts arbitrary JSON events over HTTPS. Send a POST request with a list of events; UTMStack parses them and routes through your configured parser.

auth.title: 2 · Authenticate with a federation token
auth.body: Get a federation token from Settings → Connection Key and send it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.

endpoint.title: JSON ingestion endpoint
endpoint.hint: Use this request shape from your application or a cron job. The token is the federation key from Settings → Connection Key.

openServerManager.title: 1 · Open Server Manager
openServerManager.body: On the AD domain controller, open Server Manager.

addRoles.title: 2 · Add Roles and Features
addRoles.body: Choose "Add roles and features" from the Manage menu.

selectCertServices.title: 3 · Select Active Directory Certificate Services
selectCertServices.body: On the Server Roles step, select Active Directory Certificate Services.

installServices.title: 4 · Install the Certificate Authority role service
installServices.body: On the Role Services step, select Certificate Authority and finish the wizard.

configureAdCs.title: 5 · Configure AD CS
configureAdCs.body: After install, click the notification to configure AD CS and choose Certificate Authority as the role service to configure.

pickCaType.title: 6 · Pick the CA type
pickCaType.body: Choose Enterprise CA → Root CA → Create a new private key.

setValidity.title: 7 · Set the certificate validity period
setValidity.body: Set a validity period that fits your organization (5 years is typical).

confirm.title: 8 · Confirm and install
confirm.body: Review the settings and click Configure to finish.

restart.title: 9 · Restart the domain controller
restart.body: Restart the domain controller so LDAPS becomes available on TCP 636.

activate.title: 10 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so AD audit events start flowing.

overview.title: 1 · About the vulnerabilities scanner
overview.body: The UTMStack vulnerabilities module scans assets discovered through the Asset Management module and matches their fingerprint against the CVE database.

scope.title: 2 · Define scan scope
scope.body: Use the Asset Management module to register the hosts you want scanned. The vulnerabilities scanner will run periodically against them.

activate.title: 3 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module to start scanning.

overview.title: 1 · About Asset Management
overview.body: The Asset Management module discovers and inventories hosts, software, and services across your network.

agentRequirement.title: 2 · Agent requirement
agentRequirement.body: Asset discovery uses UTMStack agents running on Linux, Windows, or macOS hosts. Install the agent on the systems you want inventoried.

activate.title: 3 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module to start asset discovery.

enableAuditPolicy.title: 1 · Enable Audit Object Access
enableAuditPolicy.body: On the Windows host, open Group Policy → Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → Object Access and enable "Audit File System".

configureFolderAuditing.title: 2 · Configure folder auditing
configureFolderAuditing.body: On each folder you want monitored, open Properties → Security → Advanced → Auditing and add an auditing entry for the principals and access types you care about.

verifyEvents.title: 3 · Verify events appear in Security log
verifyEvents.body: Open Event Viewer and confirm 4663/4670 events are being generated when the audited objects are accessed.

activate.title: 4 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so file integrity events start flowing.

overview.title: 1 · About SOC AI
overview.body: SOC AI augments UTMStack with an LLM-backed analyst that summarizes alerts and suggests next steps. It runs against the provider you configure.

chooseProvider.title: 2 · Choose a provider
chooseProvider.body: Pick a provider — OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Google Gemini, Ollama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Groq, or a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

configureCredentials.title: 3 · Configure credentials
configureCredentials.body: Provide the API key and (where applicable) the model name and endpoint URL.

activate.title: 4 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so SOC AI starts working on alerts.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: This integration self-monitors your UTMStack deployment. A lightweight collector installed on the UTMStack host tails the platform's own Docker container logs and ships them back into UTMStack for correlation and alerting.

requirements.title: Runs on the UTMStack host only
requirements.body: This integration can only be installed on a UTMStack instance running Ubuntu or a Red Hat-family distribution. Install the collector directly on the UTMStack server.

install.title: Install the collector
install.body: On the UTMStack host, pick your operating system and run the command below to download and install the self-monitoring collector:
install.sensitiveWarning: This command contains a sensitive connection token. Treat it like a password and don't share it.

after.title: What you'll see after installing
after.item1: The collector registers itself and appears under Data sources.
after.item2: UTMStack container logs start flowing within a minute.
after.item3: Events become searchable in Log Explorer under the utmstack data type.

uninstall.title: Uninstall the collector
uninstall.body: To remove the self-monitoring collector from the UTMStack host, run:

enableAuditPolicy.title: 1 · Enable Audit Object Access
enableAuditPolicy.body: On the Windows host, open Group Policy → Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → Object Access and enable "Audit File System".

configureFolderAuditing.title: 2 · Configure folder auditing
configureFolderAuditing.body: On each folder you want monitored, open Properties → Security → Advanced → Auditing and add an auditing entry for the principals and access types you care about.

activate.title: 3 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so file activity events start flowing.

openConsole.title: 1 · Open the Elastic Beanstalk console
openConsole.body: In the AWS Console, open Elastic Beanstalk.

environment.title: 2 · Open the environment management page
environment.body: Navigate to the management page for the environment you want to monitor.

software.title: 4 · Modify the Software configuration
software.body: In the Software configuration category, choose Modify.

s3LogStorage.title: 5 · Enable S3 log storage
s3LogStorage.body: Under S3 log storage, choose Rotate logs to upload rotated logs to Amazon S3.

cloudwatchStreaming.title: 6 · Enable CloudWatch Logs streaming
cloudwatchStreaming.body: Under Instance log streaming to CloudWatch Logs, enable streaming, set the retention period, and pick whether to upload existing logs.

activate.title: 7 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so Beanstalk events start flowing.

taskDefinition.title: 1 · Update your task definition
taskDefinition.body: In the task definition for the Fargate task, set the logDriver to "awslogs" and define the log group name.

cloudwatchLogs.title: 2 · Confirm CloudWatch Logs is receiving logs
cloudwatchLogs.body: Open the CloudWatch Logs console and confirm the log group is being populated when tasks run.

iamPrerequisite.title: 3 · IAM user prerequisite
iamPrerequisite.body: This integration shares credentials with the AWS IAM User module — make sure it's configured with CloudWatchLogsReadOnlyAccess.

activate.title: 4 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so Fargate events start flowing.

iamConsole.title: 1 · Open the IAM console
iamConsole.body: In the AWS console, go to IAM → Users → Add users.

createUser.title: 2 · Create the user
createUser.body: Pick a username (e.g. utmstack-ingest). Choose programmatic access.

review.title: 5 · Review the user
review.body: Review the user details and click Create user.

copyKeys.title: 6 · Copy the access key ID and secret
copyKeys.body: Copy the Access key ID and the Secret access key — the secret is shown only once.

createLogGroup.title: 7 · Create a CloudWatch log group
createLogGroup.body: In CloudWatch → Log groups, create a log group named "utmstack" — other AWS integrations will deliver to it.

fillForm.title: 8 · Fill the form
fillForm.body: Provide the access key, secret, default region, and the log group name (e.g. "utmstack") to UTMStack.

activate.title: 9 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so AWS events start flowing.

iamPrerequisite.title: 1 · IAM user prerequisite
iamPrerequisite.body: Lambda relies on the AWS IAM User module — make sure that integration is configured first with CloudWatchLogsReadOnlyAccess.

cloudwatchStream.title: 2 · Lambda already streams to CloudWatch Logs
cloudwatchStream.body: AWS Lambda automatically publishes execution logs to CloudWatch Logs under /aws/lambda/<function_name>. UTMStack ingests from the log group you configured in the IAM user setup.

activate.title: 3 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so Lambda events start flowing.

pickDb.title: 2 · Pick the DB instance
pickDb.body: In the navigation pane, choose Databases and select the DB instance you want to monitor.

logExports.title: 4 · Enable Log Exports
logExports.body: In the Log exports section, choose Error log and Agent log to publish to CloudWatch Logs.

apply.title: 5 · Apply changes
apply.body: Choose Continue, then Modify DB Instance on the summary page.

activate.title: 6 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so SQL Server events start flowing.

pickDb.title: 2 · Pick the DB instance
pickDb.body: In the navigation pane, choose Databases and select the DB instance you want to modify.

logExports.title: 3 · Enable Log Exports
logExports.body: In the Log exports section, choose the PostgreSQL log to publish to CloudWatch Logs.

apply.title: 4 · Apply changes
apply.body: Choose Continue, then Modify DB Instance on the summary page.

activate.title: 5 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so PostgreSQL events start flowing.

createTarget.title: 1 · Create a traffic mirror target
createTarget.body: In the VPC console, create a Traffic Mirror Target that points at the network interface of the UTMStack agent VM.

createFilter.title: 2 · Create a traffic mirror filter
createFilter.body: Create a Traffic Mirror Filter and add inbound/outbound rules for the protocols you want to mirror (e.g. all TCP, all UDP).

createSession.title: 3 · Create a traffic mirror session
createSession.body: Create a Traffic Mirror Session that pairs each source network interface with the target and filter you created.

iamPrerequisite.title: 4 · IAM user prerequisite
iamPrerequisite.body: Make sure the AWS IAM User module is also configured so UTMStack can read VPC flow logs if needed.

activate.title: 5 · Activate
activate.body: Activate the UTMStack module so mirrored traffic starts being parsed.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: Logs flow from {{source}} to the UTMStack Collector, which streams them securely into UTMStack for correlation and alerting. Nothing is installed on {{source}} — only the Collector needs to run on a host in your network.

forwarder.noInstall: Nothing is installed on {{source}} — you only redirect its logs to the Collector.

install.title: Install the UTMStack Collector
install.body: The Collector is a Linux service that receives logs from your devices and sends them to UTMStack. A single Collector handles multiple integrations at the same time.
install.reuse: Already have a Collector running? Skip this step — point {{source}} at the existing one using the host and port shown below.

tls.title: Optional — Enable TLS encryption
tls.intro: By default the listener accepts plain TCP/UDP. To encrypt syslog traffic in transit, load your certificate files first, then re-enable the listener with the tls protocol.
tls.step1: 1 · Load your certificate and key (once per Collector)
tls.step1Note: An optional CA certificate can be added as a third argument. Omit it to use the leaf certificate as CA.

httpsCerts.title: Load the TLS certificate on the Collector
httpsCerts.body: This integration uses an HTTPS listener on port {{port}}, so the Collector needs a certificate and key loaded before enabling it:

uninstall.title: Optional — Uninstall the Collector
uninstall.body: Run this command on the host where the Collector is installed to stop the service and remove all its files.

manualCommand.title: Optional — Enable via the command line instead
manualCommand.intro: Prefer the terminal? SSH into the Collector host and run the command below — it matches whatever protocol and port you have selected above.
manualCommand.certStep: 1 · Load your certificate and key (once per Collector)

instanceHeader.title: Authorization header
instanceHeader.body: Include this Authorization header on every request you send to the instance. The API key's secret is revealed only once when it is generated — copy it then and paste it in place of the placeholder below.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack connects to Microsoft 365 with a registered Azure AD app and polls Microsoft Graph for security events: alerts, incidents, directory audit, sign-ins, risk detections, hunting queries and Purview audit logs. No agent is installed in your tenant.
intro.note: UTMStack requires read-only Graph API access — no write permissions are requested.

azurePortal.title: Open Microsoft Entra ID
azurePortal.body: Open the <hl>Azure Portal</hl> (portal.azure.com) and click on <hl>Microsoft Entra ID</hl>.

appRegistrations.title: Go to App registrations
appRegistrations.body: In the left menu, click <hl>App registrations</hl>.

registerApp.title: Register a new app
registerApp.body: Click <hl>New registration</hl>. Name it <hl>UTMStack Graph Dev</hl>, select <hl>Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single-tenant)</hl>, and click <hl>Register</hl>.

clientSecret.title: Create a client secret
clientSecret.body: Go to <hl>Certificates & Secrets → New client secret</hl>. Add a description, set expiry to <hl>730 days (24 months)</hl>, and click <hl>Add</hl>.
clientSecret.copyNote: Copy the secret Value immediately — it is only shown once and cannot be retrieved later.

apiPermissions.title: Add Microsoft Graph permissions
apiPermissions.body: Go to <hl>API Permissions → Add a permission</hl> and select <hl>Microsoft Graph</hl>, then choose <hl>Application permissions</hl>.

adminConsent.title: Grant admin consent
adminConsent.body: Back in <hl>API Permissions</hl>, click <hl>Grant admin consent for {tenant}</hl> and confirm.

noteIds.title: Copy the app IDs
noteIds.body: Go to the app <hl>Overview</hl> and copy the <hl>Application (client) ID</hl> and <hl>Directory (tenant) ID</hl>. You also need the secret value copied in step 4.

credentials.title: Connect your Microsoft 365 tenant
credentials.body: Enter the details from the steps above. UTMStack verifies the credentials before saving. You can add multiple config groups.

cloud.howItWorksBody: {{name}} runs entirely inside UTMStack — no agent or collector to deploy. Provide read-only API credentials and UTMStack will pull events on a schedule, parse them, and ingest them into Log Explorer.
cloud.after1: UTMStack performs an initial backfill of recent events.
cloud.after2: From then on, events are pulled every 1–5 minutes (depends on the API).
cloud.after3: The integration appears under Data Sources with current pull status and lag.

tenants.title: Configured config groups
tenants.empty: No config groups configured yet. Add your first one below.
tenants.invalidJson: Could not parse the file as JSON.
tenants.createError: Could not create the config group. Please try again.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack reads audit activity directly from Google Cloud via Pub/Sub. A Logs Router sink streams your project logs into a Pub/Sub topic; UTMStack runs an internal puller that reads a Pull subscription on that topic using a service-account key. Nothing is installed in your GCP project.
intro.note: No agent runs in GCP — UTMStack pulls messages from the Pub/Sub subscription using the service-account JSON key you provide below.

createTopic.title: Create a Pub/Sub topic
createTopic.body: In the Google Cloud console, open Pub/Sub → Topics and create a new topic. The Logs Router sink will publish your project logs to it.

createSubscription.title: Create a subscription
createSubscription.body: From the topic menu, create a subscription. UTMStack pulls messages from this subscription.

configureSubscription.title: Configure the subscription
configureSubscription.body: Leave the Delivery type as Pull and the Expiration as Never expire. The default acknowledgement deadline (10s) and message retention are fine.

logsRouter.title: Open Logs Router and create a sink
logsRouter.body: Navigate to Logging → Logs Router and create a new sink. This is what forwards your project logs into the Pub/Sub topic above.

sinkDestination.title: Point the sink at the topic
sinkDestination.body: Choose Cloud Pub/Sub topic as the sink destination and select the topic you created. Optionally use inclusion/exclusion filters to scope which logs are forwarded, then create the sink.

serviceAccount.title: Create a service account
serviceAccount.body: Open IAM & Admin → Service Accounts in the project that holds your topic and sink, and create a new service account. Grant it the Pub/Sub Editor role so UTMStack can pull from the subscription.

serviceAccountKey.title: Generate a key for the service account
serviceAccountKey.body: Open the service account, go to the Keys tab, and add a new key. Choose JSON as the key type.

downloadKey.title: Download the JSON key
downloadKey.body: Save the JSON file Google downloads — its contents go in the Service account JSON key field below. The key is shown only once.

credentials.title: Pub/Sub configuration
credentials.body: Use the values collected above to configure UTMStack. You can monitor more than one project by saving additional configurations.

mapping.projectId: Project ID — the GCP project that holds your topic, subscription and sink
mapping.subscription: Subscription name — the Pull subscription created in step 2
mapping.jsonKey: Service account JSON key — the file downloaded in step 8

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack reads audit activity directly from an Azure Event Hub. You configure your Azure subscription to stream events into an Event Hub; UTMStack runs an internal puller that reads that hub and checkpoints its progress in a Storage Account. Nothing is installed in your Azure tenant.
intro.note: No agent runs in Azure — UTMStack pulls events from the Event Hub using the connection strings you provide below.

createEventHub.title: Create an Event Hub
createEventHub.body: In the Azure Portal, create an Event Hubs namespace and an Event Hub inside it. UTMStack will read events from this hub.
createEventHub.docLabel: Quickstart: Create an event hub using the Azure portal

sharedAccessPolicy.title: Add a Shared Access Policy
sharedAccessPolicy.body: Open the Event Hub → Shared access policies and create a new policy. Make sure you select the Listen permission.

connectionString.title: Copy the primary connection string
connectionString.body: Open the Shared access policy you just created and copy the Connection string–primary key. You will use it to configure your config group below.

consumerGroup.title: Create a dedicated consumer group
consumerGroup.body: Get the Consumer Group name in: All services → Event Hubs → your namespace → Event Hubs → your instance → Consumer groups. You will use it to configure your config group below.
consumerGroup.warn: Create a consumer group specifically for UTMStack. Do not use $Default or any other group already in use — reusing a consumer group across unrelated consumers can cause unexpected behavior and lost events. All UTMStack instances should share the same consumer group so they can process events together.

createStorageAccount.title: Create a Storage Account
createStorageAccount.body: UTMStack needs a Storage Account to checkpoint its read position. Create one in the same region as the Event Hub.

storageContainer.title: Get the Storage Container name
storageContainer.body: Get the Storage Container name in: All services → Storage accounts → your account → Containers. You will use it to configure your config group below.

storageConnection.title: Copy the Storage Account connection string
storageConnection.body: Get the Storage Account connection string with key in: All services → Storage accounts → your account → Access keys. UTMStack uses it to store Event Hub checkpoints.

eventGrid.title: Register the Event Grid resource provider
eventGrid.body: Configure your subscription to send logs to the Event Hub. Go to Subscriptions → Resource providers, search for Event Grid (Microsoft.EventGrid) and make sure it is registered.

createEventSubscription.title: Create an Event Subscription
createEventSubscription.body: In the subscription Events panel, create a new event by clicking Events → Event Subscription.

configureEventSubscription.title: Point the Event Subscription at your Event Hub
configureEventSubscription.body: Configure the Event Subscription to send logs to the Event Hub you created in step 1.

credentials.title: Event Hub configuration
credentials.body: Use the data collected in the steps above to configure UTMStack. You can add more than one Event Hub by saving additional configurations.

mapping.eventHubConnection: Event Hub connection string — value obtained in step 3
mapping.consumerGroup: Consumer group — value obtained in step 4
mapping.storageContainer: Storage container name — value obtained in step 6
mapping.storageConnection: Storage account connection string — value obtained in step 7

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack reads audit activity directly from AWS CloudWatch Logs. CloudTrail captures API calls and management events across your AWS account, forwards them to a CloudWatch log group, and UTMStack polls that group to ingest and correlate events.
intro.note: No agent is installed on AWS — UTMStack pulls log events using read-only IAM credentials you provide below.

dashboard.title: Open the IAM dashboard
dashboard.body: Open the AWS console, navigate to the IAM dashboard and select Users.

addUser.title: Add a user
addUser.body: Click Add user, enter a descriptive user name, and proceed to the next step.

attachPolicy.title: Attach the read-only policy
attachPolicy.body: Under Permissions, attach the required policy. Select CloudWatchLogsReadOnlyAccess for read-only CloudWatch access.

createUser.title: Create the user
createUser.body: Review the configuration and click Create user to provision the account.

openUser.title: Open the new user
openUser.body: Open the newly created user by clicking its name to view details and manage credentials.

securityTab.title: Go to Security credentials
securityTab.body: Select the Security credentials tab to create programmatic access keys.

createKey.title: Create an access key
createKey.body: Click Create access key and choose the option for an application running outside AWS (programmatic access).

confirmKey.title: Confirm creation
confirmKey.body: Confirm creation of the access key. AWS will generate an Access Key ID and Secret Access Key.

downloadKey.title: Save your credentials
downloadKey.body: Download the credentials file or copy the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key to a secure location — the Secret Access Key is only shown once.

credentials.title: Enter credentials
credentials.body: Paste the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key obtained in the previous steps. UTMStack verifies the credentials against AWS before saving.

createGroup.title: Create a CloudWatch Log Group
createGroup.body: Open the CloudWatch console, choose Log management and click Create log group.

nameGroup.title: Name the log group and set retention
nameGroup.body: Enter the log group name utmstack and set retention to 1 day. Click Create log group.

openTrail.title: Open CloudTrail and create a trail
openTrail.body: In the CloudTrail console click Create trail to begin configuring a new trail.

configureTrail.title: Configure delivery, validation and CloudWatch integration
configureTrail.body: On the CloudTrail creation form set the following options:
items: Trail name and scope: enter a descriptive name; enable Apply trail to all accounts in my organization if you need org-wide collection.
S3 destination: choose Create new S3 bucket (or select an existing bucket) for raw log delivery.
Encryption: enable Log file SSE-KMS and select the appropriate KMS key.
Log file validation: enable to ensure integrity of delivered logs (recommended).
CloudWatch Logs: enable delivery to CloudWatch, select Use existing log group and enter the exact name utmstack.
IAM role: provide or create the role CloudTrail will assume to write to S3 and publish to CloudWatch.

eventTypes.title: Select event types
eventTypes.body: Enable the event categories required for monitoring and auditing.

management.label: 1 · Management events
management.body: Enable Management events and select All to record all API activity that manages AWS resources (create, update, delete).

data.label: 2 · Data events
data.body: Add a Data event. Choose S3 and select Log all events to capture object-level operations such as GetObject and PutObject.

network.label: 3 · Network activity events
network.body: In the Network Activities section add at least one service (e.g. ec2.amazonaws.com) and enable Log all events.

review.title: Review and create the trail
review.body: On the Configure event aggregation screen accept the defaults (or adjust if required). Review all settings and click Create trail.

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: UTMStack reads detections and audit activity directly from the CrowdStrike Falcon Event Streams API. You create an API client in Falcon with Event Streams scope; UTMStack runs an internal puller that streams events using those credentials. Nothing is installed on your endpoints or in Falcon.
intro.note: No agent is deployed by UTMStack — it pulls events from Falcon using the read-only API client credentials you provide below.

apiClients.title: Open API Clients and Keys
apiClients.body: In the Falcon console, open the menu (hamburger icon, top-left) and go to Support and resources → API Clients and Keys.

createClient.title: Create a new API client
createClient.body: Click Create API Client to start a new client definition.

scopes.title: Name the client and grant Event Streams scope
scopes.body: Give the client a descriptive name (UTMStack uses it to identify the event source) and select the API scopes required for Event Streams. Click Create to generate the credentials.

recordCredentials.title: Record the credentials
recordCredentials.body: Copy the Client ID, Client Secret and the Base URL for your CrowdStrike region. The secret is shown only once — store it securely. You will paste all three into the form below.

credentials.title: API client configuration
credentials.body: Use the credentials from the steps above to configure UTMStack. You can add more than one CrowdStrike client by saving additional configurations.

mapping.appName: App name — the descriptive client name from step 3 (identifies the event source)
mapping.clientId: Client ID — value recorded in step 4
mapping.clientSecret: Client Secret — value recorded in step 4 (shown only once)
mapping.cloudRegionUrl: Base URL — your region endpoint, e.g. https://api.crowdstrike.com (us-1), https://api.us-2.crowdstrike.com (us-2), https://api.eu-1.crowdstrike.com (eu-1)

intro.title: How it works
intro.body: A custom integration ingests logs from any source the built-in modules do not cover. You install the UTMStack Collector, register a listener for your data with the protocol of your choice, and point your source at it.
intro.note: Pick the protocol your source can send (syslog UDP/TCP/TLS, or HTTP/HTTPS for JSON) below — the Collector creates the data type automatically.

choose.title: Choose protocol and port
choose.body: Select how your source sends data and the port the Collector should listen on, then run the activation command on the Collector host.
choose.tlsFirst: First load your TLS certificate and key on the Collector:
choose.authNote: To require authentication, append --auth bearer (token) or --auth hmac — the Collector prints a token to use in the Authorization header.

send.title: Point your source at the Collector
send.bodyNetwork: Configure your source to send <hl>{{proto}}</hl> syslog to <hl>{{host}}:{{port}}</hl>. Most devices have a remote-syslog or log-forwarding setting for this.
send.bodyHttp: Send your events as JSON via HTTP POST to <hl>{{endpoint}}</hl>. Each request body is one JSON event:
send.httpBindNote: The HTTP/HTTPS listener binds to 127.0.0.1 (the Collector host) by default, so post from an app running on that host — or front it with a reverse proxy. For remote sources, use syslog (UDP/TCP/TLS).

custom.parserBody: Incoming events are stored under the {{dataType}} data type. Add a parsing filter for it so the raw payload is mapped into structured fields, then build alert rules on top.

manualCommand.title: Optional — Enable via the command line instead
manualCommand.intro: Prefer the terminal? SSH into the Collector host and run the command below — it matches whatever protocol and port you have selected above.

custom.whenBody: Use this when your source is not in the catalog. Forward syslog or arbitrary JSON to UTMStack and set a parser to normalize the fields.

remoteEnable.title: Enable this integration remotely
remoteEnable.body: Pick a Collector, choose the protocol and port, then enable the integration — no SSH needed.
remoteEnable.noPermission: You don't have permission to manage remote integrations. Ask an administrator to grant the integrations.write permission.
remoteEnable.noCollectors: No Collector is registered yet. Install one above to enable integrations remotely.
remoteEnable.forwarderOffline: This Collector is offline and can't receive configuration changes right now.
remoteEnable.certLoaded: A valid certificate is already loaded on this Collector.
remoteEnable.certMissing: No certificate loaded yet — upload one to enable this protocol.
remoteEnable.certReadError: Could not read the selected file(s).
remoteEnable.secretWarning: Store this token securely — it won't be shown again.
remoteEnable.apiKeyHint: First you'll need an API key.
remoteEnable.forwarderNoRemoteControl: This forwarder was installed with remote control disabled. It ignores configuration sent from here, which can only be changed on the machine itself.

createDrawer.title: New custom integration
createDrawer.dataTypePlaceholder: Unique identifier for this data type
createDrawer.iconHint: PNG, SVG, JPEG, GIF or WEBP. Max 3MB. Used as the integration logo.
createDrawer.invalidFileType: Icon must be a valid image file (PNG, JPEG, SVG, GIF, WEBP)
createDrawer.currentIcon: Current icon — upload a file to replace it
createDrawer.name: Integration name
createDrawer.descriptionPlaceholder: What this integration ingests and why (optional)
createDrawer.nameTaken: That integration name can’t be used — an integration with that identifier already exists.
createDrawer.defaultIconNote: Default icon — upload a file to use your own.

modules.WINDOWS_AGENT: Collect Windows system, security and event-log activity through the lightweight UTMStack agent installed on each host.
modules.LINUX_AGENT: Collect Linux system, authentication and audit logs through the lightweight UTMStack agent installed on each host.
modules.MACOS: Collect macOS system and security log activity from Apple Mac endpoints through the lightweight UTMStack agent.
modules.VMWARE: Ingest VMware ESXi hypervisor syslog so virtualization-host activity and events are monitored within UTMStack.
modules.NETFLOW: Ingest NetFlow records from routers and switches to monitor network-traffic patterns and detect traffic anomalies.
modules.AWS_IAM_USER: Ingest AWS account activity and API calls via CloudTrail and CloudWatch to audit cloud usage, access and changes.
modules.AZURE: Ingest Microsoft Azure platform and activity logs to monitor cloud workloads, identity and resource changes.
modules.O365: Ingest Microsoft 365 audit logs across Exchange, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive to monitor user and admin activity.
modules.O365_GRAPH: Ingest Microsoft Graph security events — alerts, incidents, directory audit, sign-ins, risk detections and Purview audit logs — to monitor identity and threat activity across your tenant.
modules.GCP: Ingest Google Cloud Platform audit and activity logs to monitor compute, storage and identity across projects.
modules.KASPERSKY: Ingest Kaspersky Security Center detections and endpoint telemetry to correlate malware activity across the network.
modules.ESET: Ingest ESET PROTECT endpoint detections and telemetry to correlate multilayered malware defense across your estate.
modules.BITDEFENDER: Ingest Bitdefender GravityZone detections and endpoint telemetry to correlate threats across business devices.
modules.SENTINEL_ONE: Ingest SentinelOne endpoint detections and behavioral telemetry to correlate and investigate threats at scale.
modules.SOPHOS: Ingest Sophos Central detections across endpoint, server, firewall and email to correlate threats in one place.
modules.CROWDSTRIKE: Ingest CrowdStrike Falcon endpoint and workload detections to correlate cloud-native threat activity in UTMStack.
modules.CISCO: Ingest Cisco ASA firewall traffic, VPN and threat logs to monitor perimeter security and access within UTMStack.
modules.MERAKI: Ingest Cisco Meraki firewall and security-appliance syslog to monitor cloud-managed network traffic and threats.
modules.FIRE_POWER: Ingest Cisco Firepower NGFW and IPS logs to monitor intrusion attempts and threat activity at the perimeter.
modules.CISCO_SWITCH: Ingest Cisco switch syslog and telemetry to monitor network performance, configuration changes and security.
modules.FORTIGATE: Ingest Fortinet FortiGate NGFW traffic and threat logs to monitor perimeter security and network activity.
modules.FORTIWEB: Ingest Fortinet FortiWeb WAF logs to monitor web-application attacks and protect exposed services and APIs.
modules.SOPHOS_XG: Ingest Sophos XG firewall logs covering web filtering, IPS and VPN to monitor network traffic and threats.
modules.PALO_ALTO: Ingest Palo Alto Networks NGFW traffic and threat logs to monitor application usage and perimeter security.
modules.SONIC_WALL: Ingest SonicWall NGFW traffic and threat logs to monitor perimeter security and network activity in UTMStack.

overview.title: Keep track of changes and access to classified information
overview.body: File Classification enables UTMStack's built-in file activity monitoring. It tracks changes and access attempts on selected files and folders through Windows auditing. No third-party software is required.

agentInstall.title: Install the UTMStack Windows agent
agentInstall.body: Install the UTMStack agent on every Windows host that generates the audit events. No third-party software is required.

server.policyTitle: Auditing Windows Server — enable the Audit File System policy
server.policySteps:
Open Group Policy Management and edit or create a policy for the target servers.
Navigate to Computer Configuration → Policies → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Advanced Audit Policy Configuration → Audit Policies → Object Access.
Open Audit File System and enable the policy. Choose Success, Failure, or both according to your requirements.
Apply the policy to the servers you want to monitor.
server.folderTitle: Configure auditing on files and folders
server.folderIntro: Auditing must also be enabled on each file or folder you want to monitor.
server.folderSteps:
Right-click the file or folder, select Properties, then open the Security tab.
Select Advanced and open the Auditing tab.
Add an auditing entry for the users or groups to monitor. Choose successful attempts, failed attempts, or both, and specify whether the entry applies to this folder, its files, and subfolders.

desktop.policyTitle: Auditing Windows Desktop — set the Audit object access policy
desktop.policySteps:
On the primary domain controller or a system with administration tools, open Group Policy Management by running gpmc.msc.
Create a new GPO or edit an existing one. To apply it across a domain, link the GPO to the domain.
In Group Policy Management Editor, navigate to Computer Configuration → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → Audit Policy.
Open Audit object access and select Define these policy settings.
Select Success and Failure. Selecting both is recommended.
Apply the changes and close the policy dialog.
To apply the policy immediately, run Gpupdate /force in Command Prompt.
desktop.folderTitle: Set auditing on the files you want to track
desktop.folderIntro: After configuring the Group Policy, add an auditing entry to each file or folder. Auditing can be inherited by files and subfolders.
desktop.folderSteps:
In Windows Explorer, right-click the file or folder and select Properties.
Open the Security tab, select Advanced, then open the Auditing tab.
Select Add to create an auditing entry.
Select a principal and choose the users or groups whose activity you want to audit. Enter Everyone to include all users.
Choose Success, Failure, or All as the audit type. All captures both successful and failed attempts.
Under Permissions, select the actions to audit. To track file reads, include Traverse folder / Execute file, List folder / Read data, Read attributes, and Read extended attributes.
Select Full control if you want to audit all activity on the file or folder.
Confirm the entry, then apply the changes and close the open properties dialogs.

events.title: View file access events in Windows Event Viewer
events.body: Open Event Viewer and navigate to Windows Logs → Security. Use Filter Current Log to find events 4656 and 4663. Event 4663 records file access; inspect Account Name to identify the user, Logged to see when it occurred, and Object Name for the full file path.
